The problem I encountered this week was that once the pot started moving, the particles went through it.

I adjusted two things. First, I changed the collider type from Animated (Rigid) to Animated (Deforming). I also looked up the documentation to understand the difference. Because Animated (Deforming) rebuilds both the shape and velocity every frame, it takes more time to compute.

Although Animated (Rigid) is normally sufficient for rotating objects, in my case it didn’t prevent the particles from passing through. Only Animated (Deforming) worked reliably. I believe this is due to the pot rotating quickly and the particles being very close to the collision surface.

Another thing I changed the Particle Separation and Grid Scale to get better resolution. Particle Separation controls how dense the particles are, and Grid Scale affects how fine the background grid is. Lowering these values helped make the simulation more detailed and stable.

Problem:

Since the simulation is for molten platinum used in a watch strap, achieving a controlled and continuous liquid flow was challenging. The flow had to be steady but not excessive, ensuring a realistic and visually appealing effect.

One major difficulty was finding the right pot angle and circular emission size to maintain a smooth, uninterrupted stream. If the emission was too large, the liquid overflowed unnaturally; if too small, the flow became inconsistent. Another challenge was preventing the liquid edges from breaking apart or appearing chunky. Additionally, balancing fluid behavior with performance was crucial, as high particle counts significantly slowed down the simulation.
1f381247c04039c2:
Method:

To achieve a more detailed and controlled pouring effect, I adjusted the angle of the pouring cup and reduced the point separation in the pointsfromvolume node, allowing for finer particle distribution. To further refine the fluid’s appearance, I changed the operation to Gaussian in the vdbsmoothsdf node, which helped create a smoother liquid surface.

Initially, I set the sphere to continuously emit particles to generate the liquid. However, when the pot tilted, the liquid volume became excessive, leading to an unnatural flow and significantly slowing down the simulation. To resolve this, I switched to duplicating multiple spheres and having each emit particles only once. After multiple iterations and refinements, I achieved a stable and visually accurate liquid behavior that matched my intended effect.

e28e90ab3aec9ee9: The Niagara module reads VAT data by first calculating UV coordinates in a Custom HLSL node, using each particle's index and the current time to determine which pixel to sample from the VAT texture. The U and V outputs are combined into a Vector2D and fed into two texture samplers — one for the position texture and one for the color texture. The sampled position values, which are normalized between 0 and 1, are then remapped to world-space coordinates using the bounding box min and max values exported from Houdini. Finally, the results are written back to each particle's Position, Scale, and Color attributes through a Map Set node. This allows Niagara to drive hundreds of thousands of particles using pre-simulated Houdini data at real-time performance.
9eacea199c878b64: This HLSL module converts each particle's index and current time into UV coordinates for sampling the VAT texture. All key parameters are exposed as inputs, making it reusable across different VAT setups without code changes.
b8d897fb7ee92799: This node extracts position and scale data from the sampled VAT texture. The RGB channels store the particle's XYZ position, while the Alpha channel stores a uniform scale value applied equally to all three axes.

So basically, Itim passed her Houdini file to me, and I tested it. Following the tutorial, I started by writing VEX.

This is VEX code running in a Houdini Point Wrangle (Run Over set to Points). Its purpose is to rearrange a point cloud into a regular 2D grid so the point data can be baked into a texture. f24b89f3129cfdbd: This step encodes each point's 3D position as a pixel's color. Once every pixel has been processed, you get a 'position map' — an image where each pixel's RGB stores its corresponding point's XYZ coordinates. A game engine or shader can then sample this image to instantly reconstruct the entire point cloud's positions on the GPU. Other attributes can be captured in the same way.
